passages.section: Detecting Silent Action-Interface Mismatch with Calibrated Relational World Models
passages.location: Detecting Silent Action-Interface Mismatch with Calibrated Relational World Models
passages.text: A robot action can satisfy shape and range constraints yet carry the wrong semantics: axes may be permuted, signs inverted, rotations rescaled, or gripper polarity reversed. We study learned state–action–effect relations as offline contracts for detecting these mismatches and ranking their likely fields. Clean held-out transitions calibrate alarms; a fixed inverse vocabulary supports closed-set localization. On ten LIBERO Spatial tasks comprising 432 source episodes, a capacity-controlled comparison at 2.5% empirical clean false-positive rate gives 46.1% recall for a ridge forward residual, 61.0% for a four-component joint Gaussian mixture, and 65.7% for the exact conditional of that same mixture. The joint score retains a 14.9 percentage-point advantage over ridge, while conditioning improves recall by a further 4.7 points. Joint scoring instead has higher localization: 95.8% versus 94.6%. These matched-rate comparisons are retrospective diagnostics, not deployment calibration guarantees. Earlier Object/Goal results broaden tasks within the LIBERO convention; DROID, all three HYDRA tasks, short temporal faults, small offsets, exact repair, and simulated mitigation fail their respective gates, while xArm contributes one task only. The evidence supports a bounded offline diagnostic and a detection–localization tradeoff, rather than joint-density superiority or cross-robot safety.

World models usually predict dynamics or support planning. At a controller boundary, they can also ask whether an action’s semantics agree with the observed transition. A seven-dimensional action vector may mix normalized translation, axis-angle rotation and gripper commands. Components can agree on shape and bounds while disagreeing about scale, axes, signs, rotation units or polarity. Such a command is numerically legal but inconsistent with the recorded state change.

We study whether recorded state–action–next-state tuples can supply an executable contract for this failure class. A detector is trained on clean transitions, a disjoint clean split fixes its alarm threshold, and in-range semantic mutations are applied only after that calibration is frozen. After an alarm, the system evaluates a declared set of inverse transformations and reports the one that best restores relational consistency. This separates two questions that aggregate anomaly scores often conflate: whether the transition should be inspected and which contract field is the most plausible explanation.

The diagnostic addresses interface semantics, not perception, planning, contact or task progress. Replay supplies the factual next state of the original action, not the physical outcome of executing a corrupted action. We evaluate offline alarms and closed-set localization; they do not measure task success or safe correction.

The study separates three sources of apparent advantage: using the observed transition, representing multimodal clean behavior, and choosing an alarm operating point. The original joint-mixture comparison outperformed a ridge forward residual, but those methods had different achieved false-positive rates. A post-decision capacity-controlled analysis addresses both confounds. At matched empirical clean FPR, the exact conditional of the fitted mixture has higher detection recall than the joint score; the joint score retains better closed-set localization. We report that reversal alongside episode-level uncertainty and the external and closed-loop failures that bound the method’s use.

World models learn compact predictive representations for control ( Ha & Schmidhuber, 2018 ) ; here prediction is used as evidence about an interface, not as a rollout planner. Learned runtime monitors instead anticipate broad policy failures. Model-based monitoring uses interactive imitation learning ( Liu et al., 2023b ) ; Sentinel combines temporal action consistency with task progress ( Agia et al., 2024 ) ; and RAPT uses calibrated predictive deviation for deployment-time detection and diagnosis ( Munn et al., 2026 ) . These systems address general failure or distribution shift. Our scope is a declared vocabulary of controller-semantics transformations and attribution to a contract field.

Model-security work supplies a scope boundary. Backdoor detectability depends on nominal/hidden-task relation and detector assumptions ( Tang et al., 2022 ; Zhu et al., 2024 ) ; TrojAI distinguishes detection, diagnosis and mitigation ( Reese et al., 2026 ) . Backdoor suppression ( Zhu et al., 2023 ; Jiang et al., 2026 ) and model-lifecycle risks ( Chen et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2025 ; Zhu et al., 2026 ) concern different interventions. They provide no evidence for this fixed-weight interface diagnostic, and inverse ranking is neither model purification nor adaptive-attack robustness.

Action Mahalanobis distance is a natural cheap out-of-distribution baseline ( Lee et al., 2018 ) . It cannot, by construction, use the observed state change: a transformed action may remain marginally plausible while becoming inconsistent with the transition. A field-aligned static comparator can couple translation, rotation, and gripper coordinates to measured displacement, but public benchmark metadata omit the controller gains and absolute-versus-delta semantics needed for a faithful executable specification. We include both checks so that improvement is not measured only against range validation.

Robot-testing work explores a complementary axis. VLATest generates diverse manipulation scenes ( Wang et al., 2024 ) , FATE-VLA searches for failure-prone scenes ( Kanwal et al., 2026 ) , and metamorphic testing compares related executions without a task-specific oracle ( Valle et al., 2026 ) . ContractFuzz mutates action semantics rather than observations or scenes. The motivating deployment observation is that weights alone do not specify normalization and controller conventions ( Tai, 2026 ) ; our experiments test when a learned state–action relation can expose that missing contract.

A fault k k applies a transform T k : ℝ d a → ℝ d a T_{k}:\mathbb{R}^{d_{a}}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{d_{a}} . We evaluate only changed rows whose transformed action remains inside clean training bounds,

The supported set contains halving the six motion coordinates, swapping the X and Y axes, reversing the X-axis sign, shrinking rotation units, and reversing gripper polarity. A fixed X-offset is retained as an unsupported stress test. Temporal delay, half-frequency hold, and chunk reversal are evaluated separately and fail the main detector gate.

That design isolates relational inconsistency and supplies a known mutation label. The conditional mixture therefore has input-dependent component weights and conditional means, without adding parameters or fitting a separate model. Its comparison with R G R_{G} isolates the contribution of the input marginal to the score; it does not compare independently optimized model classes. A disjoint clean calibration split sets each detector’s threshold to an empirical upper quantile targeting 2.5% false positives. No mutation outcome enters model selection or threshold fitting.

For attribution, each inverse hypothesis U j U_{j} , including identity, maps the observed action back into a candidate convention. The reported candidate is the one with the lowest relational score on ( s t , U j ​ ( a ) , s t + 1 ) (s_{t},U_{j}(a),s_{t+1}) . We call Top-1 agreement with the injected field localization ; earlier logs use repair_top1 , but a correct ranking does not demonstrate executable repair.

The primary benchmark is public LIBERO ( Liu et al., 2023a ) , pinned to data revision e5907374380b8f96511957e6ba5582be52a1e179 . Episodes, not transitions, are partitioned 60/20/20 into training, calibration, and test sets for each deterministic split seed; at most 2,000 transitions are sampled per seed. The audit contains 1,243 task–episode clusters and 160,414 transitions across 30 retained Spatial, Object, and Goal tasks. Repeated split seeds reduce algorithmic Monte Carlo variation but do not create new trajectories.

External-convention screens use low-dimensional data only. DROID-100 ( Khazatsky et al., 2024 ) contributes 100 episodes and 32,112 transitions, but 46/47 task labels are singletons, so its frozen screen is pooled and episode-disjoint. The FOWM xArm Lift conversion ( Feng et al., 2023 ) contains 800 repeated episodes and 19,200 source-semantic XYZ-plus-gripper transitions from one task. Stanford HYDRA ( Belkhale et al., 2023 ) contains 570 episodes, three tasks, and 357,664 valid transitions with source-defined 7D end-effector-delta and gripper actions. Video and simulator assets are excluded. Conflicting HYDRA mirror metadata are handled conservatively by retaining the source-specific CC-BY-4.0 notice rather than interpreting license terms.

We report clean false-positive rate (FPR), mutation recall, recall gain over the named comparator, and closed-set localization Top-1. The cheap baseline is the better of a full-covariance action Mahalanobis detector and static range legality. A structured field-aligned displacement model independently fits clean affine maps from the named action coordinates to next-frame translation, relative axis-angle, and gripper aperture. The ridge forward score R f R_{f} is the original conditional baseline; the capacity-controlled conditional mixture R C R_{C} is added in the post-decision validation.

The original task gate requires FPR at most 0.05, recall gain at least 0.10 over action/static checks, and localization at least 0.70. Later mixture confirmation requires a task-median recall gain of 0.10 over ridge, wins on at least eight tasks, and both methods below 0.05 FPR. These are historical study gates, not matched-FPR comparisons. The supplement retains the aggregate gates, multiplicity correction, sensitivity results, and a run whose FPR of 0.0500375 exceeds the limit. Repeated split seeds are collapsed within source episode before paired task/episode inference; they do not create new trajectories.

A fixed protocol evaluates all ten Spatial tasks and five supported families on 100 episode-disjoint partitions per task (seeds 33001–33100), retaining the original fitting, preprocessing, transition cap and valid-row rule. No new source episodes are introduced. Each method is first evaluated at clean-calibration quantiles targeting 1%, 2.5%, and 5% FPR, with achieved test FPR reported separately. A second, retrospective diagnostic derives thresholds from held-out clean scores and interpolates adjacent clean-score cutoffs to match empirical FPR exactly. Mutation labels do not select those cutoffs. This curve compares scores; it cannot supply a test-free deployment threshold.

The primary endpoint is recall at 2.5% matched FPR, with two paired comparisons: joint minus ridge and joint minus conditional GMM. Repeated test appearances are averaged within episode–fault cells, then faults within episode, episodes within task, and ten tasks with equal weights. A paired hierarchical bootstrap uses 20,000 task/episode resamples. The reported 95% intervals are conditional on fitted scores and clean-reference thresholds; they exclude refitting and threshold-estimation uncertainty. Bonferroni 97.5% intervals for the two primary comparisons are retained in the supplement. Other FPRs and localization are descriptive endpoints.

Table 1 and Figure 1 compare the three scores without changing model capacity or empirical clean alarm rate. At 2.5% FPR, joint GMM recall is 0.6096 versus 0.4608 for ridge: the paired advantage is 0.1488, with 95% interval [ 0.1207 , 0.1798 ] [0.1207,0.1798] . The exact conditional GMM instead reaches 0.6566, exceeding joint recall on all ten tasks. Joint-minus-conditional recall is − 0.0470 -0.0470 with interval [ − 0.0632 , − 0.0350 ] [-0.0632,-0.0350] ; its two-comparison 97.5% interval [ − 0.0658 , − 0.0339 ] [-0.0658,-0.0339] also excludes zero. The conditional advantage is 0.0422 at 1% FPR and 0.0422 at 5%. The result supports multimodal relational modeling over the ridge residual, but rejects the claim that joint scoring has the best detection recall among the tested scores.

passages.section: 5.2 Calibration and localization answer different questions
passages.location: 5.2 Calibration and localization answer different questions
passages.text: At calibration-only thresholds targeting 2.5% FPR, the achieved equal-episode clean rates are 0.0263 for ridge, 0.0322 for joint GMM and 0.0285 for conditional GMM; corresponding recalls are 0.4413, 0.6086 and 0.6504. Sharing a nominal quantile or satisfying the same 5% cap therefore does not establish a matched operating point. The matched analysis removes that confound for this finite reference set while leaving clean-only deployment calibration as a separate task.

passages.section: 5.2 Calibration and localization answer different questions
passages.location: 5.2 Calibration and localization answer different questions
passages.text: Detection and attribution also rank the models differently. Closed-set localization is 0.9581 for joint GMM, 0.9462 for conditional GMM and 0.9270 for ridge. These accuracies use all valid mutated rows under the fixed inverse vocabulary. The joint score’s higher localization does not establish an end-to-end benefit after alarm selection, and its extra input-marginal term does not improve recall here.

passages.section: 5.2 Calibration and localization answer different questions
passages.location: 5.2 Calibration and localization answer different questions
passages.text: All 1,000 GMM fits converge. Each episode–fault cell has at least 12 held-out appearances, averaged before inference. The supplement reports independent conditional-density and exact-FPR interpolation checks.

The original calibration-only comparison reports a task-median joint-minus-ridge recall difference of 0.15663. A previous 432-episode analysis estimates 0.16753 [ 0.13642 , 0.20297 ] [0.13642,0.20297] . Those values remain in the supplement with their original operating points; the matched-FPR estimate of 0.1488 above is the appropriate comparison for the present detection claim. Its different seeds and estimand mean that subtracting the two estimates does not identify a causal “FPR contribution.”

Earlier joint-GMM advantages over ridge also recur within LIBERO Object and Goal, with recall differences 0.21183 and 0.17956 under their original calibration protocols. They share LIBERO’s action convention. The new conditional and matched-FPR comparisons are restricted to Spatial; they have not been repeated on those suites. A field-aligned static displacement comparator has median recall 0.32020 and localization 0.84245, below the historical joint-GMM result, but absent controller gains prevent a faithful manufacturer-specification interpretation. Complete earlier operating-point, ablation and sensitivity values remain in the supplement as historical evidence.

passages.section: 6.1 Detection, explanation, and abstention are different decisions
passages.location: 6.1 Detection, explanation, and abstention are different decisions
passages.text: Fault families vary materially. Supported transformations have median recall gains 0.300–0.452 and localization 0.878–0.966. The fixed X-offset stress test has only 0.0047 gain and 0.555 localization under the original score; the GMM also passes 0/10 offset gates with median recall 0.0340. Yet seven-candidate localization is 0.7340. In a task/episode-clustered mechanism analysis, alarm recall is 0.0328, localization is 0.7304, and localization among non-alarmed rows is 0.7388; AUROC is only 0.5475. Relative candidate evidence can therefore be informative even when the absolute clean-versus-fault distributions overlap too strongly for a high-precision alarm.

passages.section: 6.1 Detection, explanation, and abstention are different decisions
passages.location: 6.1 Detection, explanation, and abstention are different decisions
passages.text: A selection-frozen descriptive reuse of the same 432 episodes places 74.01% of offset episodes in an explanation-only false-negative stratum. For supported families, 75.51% of episode–fault cells are detected and localized, 1.05% are localized without detection, none are joint failures, and 23.43% lie in a mixed boundary region. These values explain an existing result; they are not an independent confirmation.

passages.section: 6.1 Detection, explanation, and abstention are different decisions
passages.location: 6.1 Detection, explanation, and abstention are different decisions
passages.text: An omitted-family audit cross-fits confidence thresholds between fixed task halves using only the other four supported families. Aggregate rejection of a deliberately hidden family is 0.7411, but omitted X-sign rejection is only 0.3720 and 64.67% of those rows are forced into the XY-swap label. This rejects a universal open-set guarantee. The operational rule is consequently asymmetric: an alarm can request inspection for a represented family, but no alarm cannot certify a correct interface, and a high relative score cannot safely remap an unknown fault.

passages.section: 6.2 External conventions do not validate transfer
passages.location: 6.2 External conventions do not validate transfer
passages.text: DROID-100 passes low-dimensional schema checks, yet pooled scale, swap, and sign recalls are only 0.0193, 0.0777, and 0.0865. Its sparse task identity also prevents a multi-task replication. One xArm Lift task passes a separately frozen screen: GMM recall is 0.6016 versus 0.5046 for forward, with 0.0245 mean FPR. Because all 800 episodes repeat one task, it supports only a bounded one-task offline sanity check.

passages.section: 6.2 External conventions do not validate transfer
passages.location: 6.2 External conventions do not validate transfer
passages.text: HYDRA is the decisive negative external screen. It passes compatibility gates and provides three repeated tasks with auditable action semantics, but coffee, dish-rack, and toast GMM recalls are only 0.1063, 0.1097, and 0.1213; zero tasks pass. Three bounded rescues do not reverse that outcome. The final SAGE-R sequence-aware redesign also passes 0/3 and underperforms the strongest sequence baseline on every task. These failures are immutable evidence: the workshop rewrite neither tunes on the HYDRA test set nor turns the one xArm result into cross-robot validation.

passages.section: 6.3 Replay evidence does not establish consequence or repair
passages.location: 6.3 Replay evidence does not establish consequence or repair
passages.text: Replay uses the factual next state produced by the clean action. A deterministic clean-trained response proxy lowers median task GMM recall from 0.6379 to 0.2381 on LIBERO and mean recall from 0.6105 to 0.0972 on xArm, but factual-minus-proxy recall on HYDRA is − 0.0978 / + 0.0604 / − 0.0440 -0.0978/+0.0604/-0.0440 . These learned-response diagnostics are not environment rollouts or causal effects.

passages.section: 6.3 Replay evidence does not establish consequence or repair
passages.location: 6.3 Replay evidence does not establish consequence or repair
passages.text: A small controlled simulator connects the detector to reject/hold/fallback under a fixed fault and delay budget. GMM fallback can recover success relative to no monitor, but it ties a ridge monitor and misses the GMM clean-FPR gate. It therefore does not demonstrate ContractFuzz-specific closed-loop success improvement. A separate continuous-offset repair sweep passes 0/10 gates, and linear, shrunk, quadratic, random-feature, and disjoint-task selectors all fail. Candidate ranking is useful diagnostic evidence; it is not a license to modify commands online.

Earlier ablations reject a universal best score. Forward-only and inverse-plus-forward scores both pass the original action/static gate, but their paired recall difference includes zero and forward-only localizes better. Four and eight GMM components pass the historical recall gate while two fail; calibration budgets of 100, 200 and 400 clean transitions pass. Family rankings differ, and small-offset or temporal severity sweeps cannot rescue the failed short-fault gates. The supplement retains the full numerical ablations and the distinction between predeclared comparisons and explanatory reuse.

The new conditional score is an analytic normalization of the same joint mixture. Its advantage does not establish superiority of every conditional architecture, and a separately optimized conditional mixture could behave differently. The post-decision analysis reuses the same 432 episodes, conditions uncertainty on the fitted scores and reference thresholds, and adds no robot, policy, or controller convention. Matched empirical FPR describes this finite offline reference set; production calibration and natural fault prevalence remain outside the evidence.

A multimodal state–action–effect relation can expose declared interface faults that remain numerically legal. The new comparison changes the interpretation of that result: a joint-mixture advantage over linear prediction error does not imply that modeling the joint density is better than conditioning. Here conditioning the same mixture improves recall, while the joint score ranks inverse candidates more accurately. Score choice should therefore follow the diagnostic decision and its alarm budget rather than an aggregate claim of model dominance.

A practical offline audit can pair clean calibration transitions with a declared inverse vocabulary and request inspection when an alarm occurs. It must report achieved clean FPR, detection recall and localization separately. Meeting a common FPR ceiling constrains the operating point but cannot replace a matched-rate comparison. No alarm cannot certify a correct interface, and candidate ranking cannot justify automatic command remapping. Independent robot conventions and actual counterfactual rollouts remain necessary to support broader deployment or safety claims.

The artifact records pinned data, splits, calibration rules, commands, checksums and CPU resources. The supplement retains all historical runtime and portability evidence, including the inconclusive exact-CPython-3.12.4 cross-host replay. The post-decision analysis adds no source data: 1,000 GMM fits and the conditional/ matched-FPR analysis take 40.40 seconds on one local CPU process with one BLAS/OpenMP thread (Python 3.11.2, NumPy 1.26.4, SciPy 1.13.1, scikit-learn 1.4.2). Its protocol, score arrays, episode metrics, hashes and independent aggregation audit are preserved separately from the original results.

This diagnostic could be misread as a safety certificate. We publish failures, restrict the claim to recorded replay, and do not recommend automatic correction. The evaluation uses public low-dimensional robot demonstrations. Physical deployment would require independent safety controls and oversight. Dataset license metadata are provenance facts, not legal conclusions.

Generative AI assisted research planning, software development, analysis and manuscript drafting. This revision used AI assistance for the post-decision code, mathematical checks, result interpretation, prose and figures. Authors remain responsible for verifying the evidence, citations and final text.

On locked LIBERO replay, calibrated relational scores detect and localize five numerically legal action-interface transformations. At matched empirical clean FPR, a joint GMM retains its recall advantage over ridge prediction error, but the exact conditional of that same mixture has still higher recall. Joint scoring instead has higher closed-set localization. The resulting detection–localization tradeoff, finite-episode uncertainty and negative external results support an auditable offline diagnostic for a declared vocabulary. They do not establish cross-robot generalization, closed-loop success improvement, causal safety or automatic repair.

This supplement separates the retained original study from the post-decision matched-FPR and conditional-score validation in Section 9 . The latter reuses existing source episodes and introduces new scoring/operating-point results; all other reported values retain their original evaluation contracts and are linked to project-local commands and machine-readable results in Section 7 . The positive claim remains restricted to offline replay of five declared, numerically legal action-interface transformations within the LIBERO convention . DROID and HYDRA remain negative; xArm remains a one-task sanity check; simulator mitigation, exact repair, open-set rejection, small offsets, and short temporal faults remain unsupported.

Table 1 defines how each evidence level may affect the paper. Repeated split seeds characterize an algorithm under different episode-disjoint partitions; they are not independent robot executions. The episode-clustered analysis is the inferential anchor. Analyses that reuse those episodes after inspecting earlier outcomes are explicitly descriptive. External screens probe convention transfer but do not become positive replications unless their predeclared gate passes.
Table 1: Evidence hierarchy. “May support” is deliberately narrower than what the underlying metric could be used to suggest.

An alarm is a thresholded clean-versus-mutated decision. Localization is Top-1 ranking among a fixed inverse-candidate set after an alarm score has been computed. Open-set rejection asks whether a held-out family should be rejected rather than forced into a known label. Repair asks whether an inferred continuous magnitude is accurate enough to modify an action. These are four different estimands. The paper supports the first two for represented LIBERO families and does not collapse them into a claim about open-set coverage, action correction, or task success.

Calibration uses an empirical upper quantile with method=higher ; mutation labels and outcomes are unavailable to fitting, model selection, and threshold choice.

The first 200-seed GMM screen is retained separately: recall wins on 10/10 tasks, but task 4 has clean FPR 0.0500375, exceeding 0.05 by 0.0000375. Its classification is inconclusive/near-boundary , not pass. The fresh 1,000-seed run was predeclared before its outcomes were inspected and passes without relying on rounding.

The frozen extension within LIBERO changes task content but not action convention. On Object, GMM-minus-forward recall is 0.21183 with task-bootstrap interval [ 0.2016 , 0.2218 ] [0.2016,0.2218] ; GMM localization is 0.9521, advantage 0.02888, and maximum FPR 0.0346. On Goal, the corresponding values are 0.17956 [ 0.1743 , 0.1849 ] [0.1743,0.1849] , 0.9525, 0.02758, and 0.0288. These are within-convention suite confirmations, not independent robot evidence.

The predeclared estimand first averages repeated test appearances for each episode–fault cell, then averages faults within episode and episodes within task, and finally assigns equal weight to each of ten Spatial tasks. The paired hierarchical bootstrap resamples tasks and then source episodes within task for 100,000 draws. Split-randomization replicates are collapsed and are never counted as independent clusters.

The family contains exactly three directional comparisons: GMM-minus-forward recall, GMM-minus-forward localization, and GMM-minus-joint localization. Table 5 reports ordinary paired 95% intervals, one-sided family-wise lower bounds using α / 3 \alpha/3 , and exact task-sign-flip tests with Holm correction. All three lower bounds are positive. Each immutable episode appears in at least 11 test splits; all 1,000 task-level GMM fits converge; maximum task-mean clean FPR is 0.0444.
Table 5: Fresh 432-episode Spatial effects. The sign-flip family has ten paired task summaries, so its smallest attainable unadjusted one-sided value is 1/1024.

An unchanged attempt to extend this clustered protocol to all suites aborts before inference because Object task 5, split seed 25221, contains zero valid gripper-polarity test rows under the locked valid-row rule. The evaluator is not altered after that observation. Consequently, no episode-clustered Object/Goal claim is made; only the earlier locked task-bootstrap suite confirmation is reported.

This is a real falsification of the earlier forward-dominance hypothesis, not an ablation removed after the mixture became favorable.

The earlier forward OFAT audit shows the same need to bind claims to an operating point. The locked baseline has gain 0.3763, localization 0.9297, and FPR 0.0314. Budgets of 500 and 1,000 preserve the ordering (gains 0.3639 and 0.3678). A 1% target lowers gain to 0.2858 and FPR to 0.0162. A nominal 5% target raises gain to 0.4389 but produces FPR 0.0601 and fails. Ridge values 10 − 4 10^{-4} and 10 − 2 10^{-2} are identical at reported precision. Mild versus severe transformations yield gains 0.2790 and 0.4362. Threshold and severity are therefore experimental factors, not post-hoc knobs.

In the fresh episode-clustered audit, alarm recall is 0.03282, localization 0.73042, localization among non-alarmed rows is 0.73881, and alarm AUROC is 0.54746. Thus a relative candidate can rank correctly even when the absolute score cannot separate clean from corrupted rows. A selection-frozen reuse places 74.01% of episodes in an explanation-only false-negative stratum. This mechanism result is descriptive , not independent confirmation.

A post-hoc delay severity curve rises sharply at four, eight, and sixteen frames (gains 0.2926/0.7179/0.9209), but it explains rather than rescues the frozen short-delay failure.

passages.location: 6.3 Factual replay is not counterfactual consequence
passages.text: In replay, the next state is the factual outcome of the original clean action, not the outcome that the transformed command would have produced. A deterministic clean-trained response proxy reduces median GMM recall from 0.6379 to 0.2381 on LIBERO and mean recall from 0.6105 to 0.0972 on xArm, but HYDRA factual-minus-proxy effects are − 0.0978 / + 0.0604 / − 0.0440 -0.0978/+0.0604/-0.0440 . passages.section: 6.3 Factual replay is not counterfactual consequence
passages.location: 6.3 Factual replay is not counterfactual consequence
passages.text: The smallest controlled simulator compares no monitor, ridge, GMM, and oracle under the same injected faults and response-delay budget. Ridge and GMM both improve success from 0.333 to 1.000, so the ContractFuzz-specific difference is exactly zero; GMM clean FPR is 0.08 and misses the 0.05 gate. Continuous-offset repair also passes 0/10 gates (median within-0.01 accuracy 0.4930). These results support neither a detector-specific closed-loop benefit nor automatic action correction.

passages.section: What would change the scientific conclusion.
passages.location: What would change the scientific conclusion.
passages.text: Widening requires new evidence: multiple independent tasks under a second auditable action convention, predeclared advantage over the strongest sequence baseline, and a real counterfactual environment where mitigation improves task success under the same fault and delay budget. These nontrivial extensions are outside this rewrite; more split seeds, post-failure threshold changes, or descriptive trajectory selection cannot substitute for them.

passages.location: 9.1 Protocol, data reuse, and exact conditional score
passages.text: This analysis was specified after the PC decision and before observing its new outputs. It reuses all 432 original Spatial source episodes and is not an independent replication. Ten tasks, five supported fault families, the original valid-row rule, training standardization, ridge regularization and four-component full-covariance GMM are unchanged. Each task uses 100 episode-disjoint 60/20/20 partitions with seeds 33001–33100 and the original 2,000-transition cap. All 1,000 GMM fits converge; each episode–fault cell has at least 12 held-out appearances. No mutation outcome selects a seed, component count, threshold or reported family.

Calibration-only thresholds use the original upper empirical clean-calibration quantile with method=higher . Achieved test FPR is reported, not assumed from the nominal target. Separately, each fitted score is evaluated against its held-out clean reference: adjacent clean-score cutoffs are interpolated to give exact empirical FPR at the specified targets. The interpolation coefficients use clean scores only; no mutant score chooses a cutoff. The maximum numerical FPR error is 1.2 × 10 − 16 1.2\times 10^{-16} , including tied-score self-checks.

Matched FPR is transition-weighted within each held-out clean split. Mutation recall averages within episode–fault cells across repeated held-out appearances, then equally over faults, episodes and tasks. Calibration-only test FPR in Table 12 uses that equal-episode aggregation. These weighting choices are explicit: a 2.5% matched clean-reference rate is not a claim that each episode individually has a 2.5% alarm rate. Reference thresholds are used only for retrospective score comparison, not proposed as deployable thresholds.

Because that restriction followed a family audit, we retain the six-family result and describe the five-family result as evidence-driven claim narrowing, not a replacement of the predeclared aggregate.

The forward model has median recall 0.4504 versus 0.3560 for the joint Gaussian and wins recall on all ten tasks, but it has lower localization on all ten: medians are 0.9285 and 0.9420. Maximum FPR is 0.0282 for forward and 0.0439 for joint. Thus the joint comparison rejects the original notion that a conditional residual dominates on both metrics; it reveals a calibrated recall–localization Pareto tradeoff.

Under this original ridge comparison, a deterministic four-component GMM is stronger. On 1,000 fresh split seeds, it beats forward recall on all ten tasks by 0.15663 in the task median while keeping maximum FPR at 0.03994. A separate localization confirmation reaches 0.95926 and beats forward by 0.02932, with paired-task 95% interval [ 0.02472 , 0.03553 ] [0.02472,0.03553] ; it beats joint Gaussian by 0.01728 [ 0.01398 , 0.01971 ] [0.01398,0.01971] . Again, these suites share the LIBERO convention.

Component sensitivity is not uniform. Four and eight components pass with median recall advantages 0.16093 and 0.16341, but two components reach only 0.07252 with interval [ 0.04073 , 0.11486 ] [0.04073,0.11486] and fail the frozen gate. Localization remains above 0.956. By contrast, nested calibration caps of 100, 200, and 400 clean transitions all pass: recall advantages are 0.14526–0.15400, localization is 0.96069, and the largest FPR is 0.04123. The evidence supports a multimodal density under modest calibration budgets, not mixture-count invariance.

On 500 unseen split seeds per Spatial task, forward-only, inverse-only, and combined variants all pass the action/static gate. The combined score raises paired median recall by only 0.0065 over forward, with a task-bootstrap 95% interval [ − 0.0042 , 0.0282 ] [-0.0042,0.0282] that includes zero. Forward-only localization is higher on all ten tasks: combined-minus-forward has paired median − 0.0053 -0.0053 , interval [ − 0.0094 , − 0.0026 ] [-0.0094,-0.0026] . The original study therefore retained forward-only as its parsimonious ridge conditional baseline. This ablation does not privilege a deterministic mechanism, because the later GMM comparison shows an advantage over ridge under the original calibration contract. The post-decision conditional comparison does not support joint-density superiority.

The original methods share a calibration quantile and a 5% test-FPR ceiling, but their achieved operating points differ. Forward and joint-Gaussian maximum clean FPRs are 0.0282 and 0.0439; forward and mixture maxima in the passing confirmation are 0.02763 and 0.03994. These ceilings do not establish a matched-FPR advantage. Section 9 supplies that comparison and the capacity-controlled conditional baseline. The earlier 200-split mixture screen reaches 0.0500375 and remains inconclusive under its frozen gate.

The forward-versus-joint tradeoff is transformation-dependent. Forward is better on both recall and localization for scale, with +0.2620 recall and +0.0098 localization; joint is better on both for X-sign, with +0.0242 recall and +0.0277 localization. Only rotation shrink satisfies the frozen material Pareto gate. A paired task bootstrap makes the limits sharper: scale recall remains directional at [ 0.2263 , 0.3125 ] [0.2263,0.3125] , but its localization interval [ − 0.0181 , 0.0019 ] [-0.0181,0.0019] crosses zero; for X-sign, joint localization remains directional at [ 0.0207 , 0.0319 ] [0.0207,0.0319] , while the recall interval crosses zero. Aggregate detector rankings therefore should not be read as uniform family dominance.

Fault magnitude changes explanation before it changes detection. For X offsets of 0.01, 0.025, 0.05, 0.10, and 0.20, GMM recall is 0.0305/0.0314/0.0330/0.0424/0.1518 while exact-magnitude localization rises from 0.4710 to 0.9490. The curve is monotone but was run after the failed offset screen, so it is mechanism evidence rather than a rescued supported family. Temporal severity behaves similarly: forward-minus-action recall gain rises from 0.0049/0.0359 at one/two frames to 0.2926/0.7179/0.9209 at four/eight/sixteen frames. Severe misalignment becomes detectable, while the short, smoother latency most relevant to deployment remains unsupported. A learned temporal baseline using ( s t , a t − 1 ) (s_{t},a_{t-1}) also passes 0/10 short-temporal gates, which rules out only that simple feature omission, not richer sequence monitoring.

Task-held-out triplets pass 3/3 with median recall gain 0.1740, localization 0.7760, and maximum FPR 0.0143. Object and Goal repeats strengthen within-LIBERO task breadth. They do not change the action representation or data-collection convention. For the same reason, 4,000 deterministic split seeds cannot substitute for 4,000 new episodes. The 432-episode clustered estimand was the original headline interval because it makes that dependency explicit. The attempted all-task clustered extension is retained as a protocol failure rather than silently changing its fault vocabulary when one Object task has no valid gripper-polarity rows.

We use an evidence hierarchy to prevent reuse from widening the claim. Fresh splits under the frozen evaluator establish algorithmic ordering on recorded tasks. Episode-clustered analyses change the inferential unit and support only the Spatial effect for which the gate is well-defined. Selection-frozen reuses diagnose heterogeneity, false negatives, and candidate confusion. Post-hoc severity curves explain a failed family. External screens test whether the same contract survives a new convention. These levels answer different questions; none converts a descriptive mechanism audit into an independent robot or task replication.
